subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — The Holocaust, Genocide & Memory
subtitle: The Holocaust, Nazi persecution, the responses of bystanders, and why we must remember genocide.

data.targetWord: the systematic persecution and murder of six million Jewish people by Nazi Germany and its collaborators during the Second World War

examples.en-GB: The Holocaust developed over years through discrimination, exclusion, violence and ultimately mass murder.

data.targetWord: the planned attempt to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group

examples.en-GB: The United Nations Genocide Convention of 1948 defined genocide and made it an international crime.

data.targetWord: hostility, prejudice or discrimination against Jewish people

examples.en-GB: Antisemitism had existed in Europe for centuries before the Nazis used it as the foundation of their ideology.

data.targetWord: the beliefs of the Nazi Party, including extreme nationalism, racism, antisemitism and the false idea of racial superiority

examples.en-GB: Nazi ideology falsely classified people into racial categories and used propaganda to spread hatred.

data.targetWord: laws introduced in Nazi Germany in 1935 that removed citizenship from Jewish people and made antisemitic discrimination part of the legal system

examples.en-GB: The Nuremberg Laws stripped Jewish people of citizenship rights and banned marriage between Jewish and non-Jewish Germans.

data.targetWord: the November Pogrom of 9–10 November 1938, a violent organised attack on Jewish homes, businesses and synagogues across Germany and Austria

examples.en-GB: Kristallnacht marked a major escalation of persecution as violence against Jews became open and widespread.

data.targetWord: a sealed area of a city where Jewish people were forced to live in overcrowded and dangerous conditions under Nazi occupation

examples.en-GB: The Warsaw Ghetto held hundreds of thousands of Jewish people in terrible conditions before deportations began.

data.targetWord: the forced removal of people from one place to another by state authorities; during the Holocaust, Jewish people were deported to ghettos, camps and killing sites

examples.en-GB: Deportation of Jewish people to extermination camps accelerated after the Wannsee Conference of 1942.

data.targetWord: a camp where people were imprisoned without legal rights; conditions were brutal and prisoners were used for forced labour

examples.en-GB: Dachau was one of the first concentration camps, opened in 1933 to hold political prisoners.

data.targetWord: a killing centre built primarily for mass murder, such as Treblinka, Sobibor and Auschwitz-Birkenau

examples.en-GB: Extermination camps were designed to kill large numbers of people quickly using gas chambers.

data.targetWord: mobile killing units that followed the German army into eastern Europe and the Soviet Union, murdering Jewish people and others in mass shootings

examples.en-GB: Einsatzgruppen carried out the systematic murder of Jewish communities across occupied Soviet territories.

data.targetWord: a person, group or government that helped Nazi Germany carry out persecution, occupation or murder

examples.en-GB: Some local police forces became collaborators by helping to identify and deport Jewish people.

data.targetWord: someone who was aware that persecution was happening but did not take direct action to help or oppose it

examples.en-GB: Historians study bystanders carefully, considering what they knew, what choices they had, and what risks were involved.

data.targetWord: someone who helped persecuted people survive, often at great personal risk, by hiding them, providing false papers or helping them escape

examples.en-GB: Rescuers often worked in networks rather than alone, providing food, shelter and false documents to Jewish people.

data.targetWord: someone who opposed Nazi rule or persecution, through armed, cultural, spiritual, political or practical means

examples.en-GB: Jewish resisters in the Warsaw Ghetto staged an armed uprising in 1943 against Nazi attempts to destroy the ghetto.

data.targetWord: a personal account given by someone who experienced an event; survivor testimony is important historical evidence

examples.en-GB: Survivor testimony must be used respectfully and alongside other historical sources when studying the Holocaust.

data.targetWord: the false claim that the Holocaust did not happen or that key facts about it are untrue; not a valid historical interpretation because it ignores overwhelming evidence

examples.en-GB: Holocaust denial is harmful because it disrespects victims and spreads false information contrary to the historical evidence.

data.targetWord: unfair, cruel or violent treatment of people because of their identity, beliefs, background or actions

examples.en-GB: Persecution of Jewish people escalated gradually through exclusion, violence, deportation and murder.

data.targetWord: a January 1942 meeting at which senior Nazi officials coordinated plans for the mass murder of Europe's Jewish population

examples.en-GB: The Wannsee Conference showed that the Holocaust was a planned, organised policy of genocide.

data.targetWord: post-war trials held in 1945–46 at which some Nazi leaders were prosecuted for war crimes and crimes against humanity

examples.en-GB: The Nuremberg Trials established the principle that individuals could be held responsible for crimes against humanity.

data.targetWord: a 1943 armed revolt by Jewish fighters in the Warsaw Ghetto against Nazi attempts to destroy the ghetto and deport its remaining inhabitants

examples.en-GB: The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising demonstrated Jewish resistance and agency even in conditions of extreme persecution.

data.targetWord: the ability of individuals to make choices and take action, even when circumstances are extremely restricted

examples.en-GB: Agency helps explain how Jewish people preserved culture, kept diaries and helped each other under persecution.

data.targetWord: a Nazi camp complex in occupied Poland that served as both a forced labour camp and a mass murder centre during the Holocaust

examples.en-GB: Auschwitz-Birkenau was the largest Nazi camp complex and became a symbol of the Holocaust.

data.targetWord: a state that organises its laws and policies around racist ideas about who belongs, with Nazi Germany classifying and excluding people based on false racial categories

examples.en-GB: Nazi Germany became a racial state after 1933 by using laws, propaganda and violence to target Jewish people.

data.targetWord: the 1948 United Nations agreement that defined genocide and made it an international crime

examples.en-GB: The UN Genocide Convention was partly a response to the Holocaust and aimed to prevent future genocides.

data.sentence: The Holocaust was the systematic persecution and murder of six million ____ people by Nazi Germany.
The ____ of 1935 removed citizenship rights from Jewish people and made antisemitism official state policy.
The violent attack on Jewish homes and synagogues on 9–10 November 1938 is known as ____ or the November Pogrom.
In January 1942, senior Nazi officials met at the ____ to coordinate the mass murder of European Jews.
Mobile killing units called ____ followed the German army into the Soviet Union and murdered Jewish communities.
Jewish people in occupied Poland were forced into overcrowded sealed areas called ____.
Someone who helped Nazi Germany carry out persecution by identifying or deporting Jewish people was called a ____.
The Warsaw Ghetto ____ of 1943 was an armed revolt by Jewish fighters against Nazi deportation.
The ____ Trials of 1945–46 prosecuted some Nazi leaders for war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Holocaust ____ is not a valid historical interpretation because it ignores overwhelming evidence.
Hostility, prejudice or discrimination specifically against Jewish people is called ____.
____, such as Treblinka and Sobibor, were built primarily for the mass murder of Jewish people.
A personal account given by someone who experienced an event is called ____.
Hitler became Chancellor of Germany in ____, allowing the Nazis to begin turning it into a dictatorship.
Rescuers often worked in ____ rather than alone, combining resources to hide and protect Jewish people.
Germany invaded Poland in September ____, bringing millions more Jewish people under Nazi occupation.
The UN ____ Convention of 1948 defined genocide and made it an international crime.

data.title: Order the escalation of Nazi persecution of Jewish people
items: 1933 — Hitler becomes Chancellor; boycott of Jewish shops and early concentration camps
1935 — Nuremberg Laws remove citizenship rights from Jewish people
1938 — Kristallnacht: open violence against Jewish communities
1941 — Einsatzgruppen carry out mass shootings in occupied Soviet Union
1942 — Wannsee Conference coordinates deportation and mass murder

data.title: Order key post-war events in Holocaust memory and justice
items: 1944–45 — Allied forces liberate camps and find survivors
1945–46 — Nuremberg Trials prosecute some Nazi leaders
1948 — UN Genocide Convention defines and criminalises genocide
Post-1948 — Memorials, museums and survivor testimony preserve memory
Present — Holocaust education and commemoration challenge denial and distortion

Warsaw Ghetto Uprising 1943: armed resistance against Nazi forces
